name: Topology on a set
statement: A topology on X is a collection of subsets of X containing the empty set and X, closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections.
conditions: T is a collection of subsets of X.
Empty set and X belong to T.
Every union of members of T belongs to T.
Every finite intersection of members of T belongs to T.
conclusion: T is a topology on X, and the pair (X,T) is a topological space.
typical_uses: Check whether a proposed family of open sets defines a topology.
Repair a proof by verifying closure under arbitrary unions and finite intersections separately.
common_misuses: Checking only finite unions instead of arbitrary unions.
Checking arbitrary intersections instead of finite intersections as a required axiom.
bridge_lemmas: The empty union is empty and the empty finite intersection is X under standard conventions.
repair_templates: Add explicit verification that an arbitrary indexed union of proposed open sets is again in the family.

name: Closed set as complement of open set
statement: A subset A of a topological space X is closed exactly when X\A is open.
conditions: A is a subset of X.
conclusion: A is closed in X iff X\A is open in X.
typical_uses: Convert closed-set claims into open-complement claims.
Diagnose proofs that confuse closed in X with closed in a larger ambient space.
common_misuses: Assuming every set is either open or closed but not both.
Taking complements in the wrong ambient space.
bridge_lemmas: Relative complements satisfy X\(union A_i)=intersection (X\A_i) and X\(intersection A_i)=union (X\A_i).
repair_templates: Specify the ambient space before taking complements and restate closedness relative to that space.

name: Closed set closure properties
statement: In a topological space, arbitrary intersections of closed sets are closed, finite unions of closed sets are closed, and the empty set and whole space are closed.
conditions: Each F_i is closed in X.
conclusion: Intersection_i F_i is closed in X, F_1 union ... union F_n is closed in X, and empty set and X are closed.
typical_uses: Prove a set is closed by representing it as an intersection of closed sets or a finite union of closed sets.
Find an error when a proof uses infinite unions of closed sets without extra justification.
common_misuses: Concluding an arbitrary union of closed sets is closed.
Forgetting that the complement is taken in X.
bridge_lemmas: Use De Morgan laws and the open-set axioms.
repair_templates: Replace an invalid infinite closed-union step with a complement/open-intersection argument or add a special argument for the union.

name: Finer and coarser topologies
statement: A topology T' on X is finer than T when every T-open set is T'-open; equivalently, T is coarser than T'.
conditions: T and T' are topologies on the same set X.
T is a subset of T' as collections of subsets.
conclusion: T' is finer than T and T is coarser than T'.
typical_uses: Compare continuity under two topologies on the same set.
Repair arguments that reverse the direction of inclusion between topologies.
common_misuses: Saying finer means fewer open sets.
Changing the underlying set while comparing topologies.
bridge_lemmas: The identity map from (X,T') to (X,T) is continuous exactly when T' is finer than T.
repair_templates: Check inclusion of open-set collections directly and reverse the claimed finer/coarser wording if needed.

name: Basis criterion
statement: A collection B of subsets of X is a basis if it covers X and whenever x lies in B1 cap B2, some B3 in B contains x and is contained in B1 cap B2.
conditions: B is a collection of subsets of X.
For every x in X, some B in B contains x.
For all B1,B2 in B and x in B1 cap B2, there is B3 in B with x in B3 subset B1 cap B2.
conclusion: B generates a topology whose open sets are exactly unions of elements of B.
typical_uses: Verify that intervals, balls, or rectangles form a basis.
Repair a proposed basis proof missing the local refinement condition.
common_misuses: Requiring B1 cap B2 itself to be a basis element when a smaller basis element is enough.
Forgetting the covering condition.
bridge_lemmas: A set U is open in the generated topology iff each point of U lies in a basis element contained in U.
repair_templates: At a point in an intersection, construct a smaller basic neighborhood contained in the intersection.

name: Topology generated by a basis
statement: Given a basis B on X, the topology generated by B consists of all subsets U of X such that every point of U lies in some B in B with B subset U.
conditions: B is a basis for X.
U is a subset of X.
conclusion: U is open in the topology generated by B iff each x in U has a basic neighborhood B_x with x in B_x subset U.
typical_uses: Prove openness by finding basic neighborhoods pointwise.
Diagnose proofs that only show every point has a neighborhood meeting U.
common_misuses: Showing a basis element intersects U rather than is contained in U.
Using a family that has not been proved to be a basis.
bridge_lemmas: U equals the union of all basis elements contained in U.
repair_templates: For each chosen point, shrink the candidate basic set until it is contained in U.

name: Comparing topologies from bases
statement: If B and B' are bases on X, then the topology from B' is finer than the topology from B iff each B-basic neighborhood of each point contains a B'-basic neighborhood of that point.
conditions: B and B' are bases on the same set X.
For every x in X and every B in B with x in B, there is B' in B' such that x in B' subset B.
conclusion: The topology generated by B' is finer than the topology generated by B.
typical_uses: Compare metric, order, product, and standard topologies.
Repair a topology-comparison proof by reducing it to basic neighborhoods.
common_misuses: Checking only that every B' element contains a B element, which proves the opposite inclusion.
Ignoring the point x in the refinement condition.
bridge_lemmas: Every open set is a union of basis elements.
repair_templates: Rewrite the comparison as a pointwise shrinking problem for basic neighborhoods.

name: Topology generated by a subbasis
statement: A subbasis S for X generates the topology whose basis consists of all finite intersections of elements of S, together with X when needed.
conditions: S is a collection of subsets of X whose union is X, or X is included by convention.
B is the collection of finite intersections of members of S.
conclusion: B is a basis and the topology generated by S is the topology generated by B.
typical_uses: Prove continuity by checking inverse images of subbasic open sets.
Build product topologies using coordinate projection subbases.
common_misuses: Allowing arbitrary intersections of subbasic sets as basic open sets.
Forgetting that finite intersections are required.
bridge_lemmas: Preimages preserve finite intersections and arbitrary unions.
repair_templates: Replace an arbitrary subbasic-intersection claim with a finite-intersection argument or prove openness by taking unions of finite intersections.

name: Order topology basis
statement: For a linearly ordered set with more than one element, the order topology is generated by open intervals and the appropriate initial or final rays at endpoints.
conditions: X is a linearly ordered set.
X has the order topology generated by intervals and endpoint rays.
conclusion: Basic open neighborhoods are open intervals, or rays of the form [minimum,b) and (a,maximum] when endpoints exist.
typical_uses: Analyze openness and convergence in ordered spaces.
Repair proofs that use Euclidean interval intuition in a non-real ordered set.
common_misuses: Forgetting endpoint-ray basis elements when a least or greatest element exists.
Assuming every order topology is metrizable or has real-like density.
bridge_lemmas: Given x in an order-open set, choose a basis interval or endpoint ray around x contained in the set.
repair_templates: At endpoints, use the correct ray-shaped basic neighborhood instead of an ordinary two-sided interval.

name: Product topology on two spaces
statement: For spaces X and Y, the product topology on X x Y has basis all products U x V with U open in X and V open in Y.
conditions: X and Y are topological spaces.
conclusion: Sets U x V form a basis for the product topology on X x Y.
typical_uses: Prove a subset of a product is open by finding open rectangles around points.
Repair product-space arguments that use arbitrary open sets as if they were rectangles.
common_misuses: Assuming every open subset of X x Y is a single product U x V.
Using U x V with U or V not open.
bridge_lemmas: Every product-open set is a union of basic open rectangles.
repair_templates: Replace a claim that W equals one rectangle by a pointwise rectangle containment argument.

name: Subspace topology
statement: If Y is a subset of X, the subspace topology on Y consists of all intersections Y cap U where U is open in X.
conditions: Y is a subset of X.
conclusion: A subset V of Y is open in Y iff V=Y cap U for some open subset U of X.
typical_uses: Translate relative openness into ambient openness.
Diagnose errors where open in Y is treated as open in X.
common_misuses: Concluding every set open in a subspace is open in the ambient space.
Using X\V instead of Y\V for relative closedness.
bridge_lemmas: If V is open in Y and Y is open in X, then V is open in X.
repair_templates: Insert the representation V=Y cap U and keep all complements relative to Y.

name: Closed sets in a subspace
statement: A subset A of a subspace Y is closed in Y exactly when A=Y cap C for some closed subset C of the ambient space X.
conditions: Y is a subspace of X.
A is a subset of Y.
conclusion: A is closed in Y iff there exists C closed in X with A=Y cap C.
typical_uses: Prove relative closedness without proving ambient closedness.
Repair proofs that identify closed-in-subspace with closed-in-ambient.
common_misuses: Assuming closed in Y implies closed in X without Y closed in X.
Taking complements in X rather than in Y.
bridge_lemmas: Y\A equals Y cap (X\C) when A=Y cap C.
repair_templates: If ambient closedness is needed, add the hypothesis that Y is closed in X or prove A is closed in X separately.

name: Closure of a set
statement: The closure of A in X is the intersection of all closed subsets of X that contain A.
conditions: A is a subset of X.
conclusion: cl_X(A) is closed, contains A, and is contained in every closed set containing A.
typical_uses: Prove minimality of closure.
Repair proofs that need the smallest closed superset property.
common_misuses: Assuming closure distributes over arbitrary unions.
Forgetting the ambient space in cl_X(A).
bridge_lemmas: The intersection of any family of closed sets is closed.
repair_templates: State the ambient space and use minimality: if A subset F and F is closed, then cl_X(A) subset F.

name: Closure by neighborhoods
statement: A point x lies in the closure of A iff every open neighborhood of x intersects A.
conditions: A is a subset of X.
conclusion: x in cl_X(A) iff every open set U with x in U satisfies U cap A nonempty.
typical_uses: Prove or refute membership in a closure by testing neighborhoods.
Repair a closure proof missing the arbitrary-neighborhood quantifier.
common_misuses: Showing only one neighborhood intersects A.
Using neighborhoods in a different topology or subspace without saying so.
bridge_lemmas: If some open neighborhood U of x misses A, then X\U is a closed set containing A but not x.
repair_templates: Replace a sequence-style argument with the neighborhood criterion unless first-countability or metric hypotheses are available.

name: Limit point
statement: A point x is a limit point of A if every neighborhood of x meets A at some point different from x.
conditions: A is a subset of X.
conclusion: x is a limit point of A iff every open neighborhood U of x contains a point of A\{x}.
typical_uses: Check whether a closure point is forced by nearby distinct points.
Repair confusion between belonging to A and being a limit point of A.
common_misuses: Allowing the point x itself to be the only point of A in every neighborhood.
Assuming every point of A is a limit point.
bridge_lemmas: x is in cl(A) iff x is in A or x is a limit point of A.
repair_templates: When using a limit point, explicitly find a point y in U cap A with y not equal x.

name: Closed iff contains limit points
statement: A subset A of X is closed iff it contains all of its limit points.
conditions: A is a subset of X.
conclusion: A is closed in X iff every limit point of A belongs to A.
typical_uses: Prove closedness using limit points.
Repair a closedness proof that proves only sequential closedness in a non-metric space.
common_misuses: Using sequence convergence as an equivalent condition in an arbitrary topological space.
Forgetting limit points may lie outside A.
bridge_lemmas: cl(A)=A union A', where A' is the set of limit points of A.
repair_templates: If the proof uses sequences, either add first-countable or metric hypotheses, or switch to open-neighborhood limit points.

name: Continuity by open preimages
statement: A function f:X->Y is continuous iff the inverse image of every open subset of Y is open in X.
conditions: X and Y are topological spaces.
f is a function from X to Y.
conclusion: f is continuous iff for every open V subset Y, f^{-1}(V) is open in X.
typical_uses: Check continuity in arbitrary topological spaces.
Repair epsilon-style arguments in non-metric settings.
common_misuses: Checking images of open sets instead of inverse images.
Forgetting that f must be defined on all of X.
bridge_lemmas: Inverse images commute with arbitrary unions and finite intersections.
repair_templates: Replace an image-openness claim with the corresponding inverse-image computation.

name: Continuity by closed preimages
statement: A function is continuous iff the inverse image of every closed set in the codomain is closed in the domain.
conditions: X and Y are topological spaces.
conclusion: f is continuous iff f^{-1}(C) is closed in X for every closed C subset Y.
typical_uses: Prove continuity when closed sets have simpler descriptions.
Repair proofs that incorrectly use images of closed sets.
common_misuses: Assuming continuous maps send closed sets to closed sets without extra hypotheses.
Taking preimages of subsets not in the codomain.
repair_templates: Use complement identities to convert an open-preimage proof into a closed-preimage proof.

name: Continuity by basis elements
statement: If B is a basis for Y, then f:X->Y is continuous iff f^{-1}(B) is open in X for every B in B.
conditions: X and Y are topological spaces.
B is a basis for the topology on Y.
conclusion: f is continuous iff all inverse images of basis elements of Y are open in X.
typical_uses: Reduce continuity checks to intervals, balls, rectangles, or subbasic neighborhoods.
Repair overlong continuity checks by testing only a basis.
common_misuses: Testing a basis for the domain instead of the codomain.
Testing images of basis elements.
bridge_lemmas: Every open set in Y is a union of basis elements and inverse images preserve unions.
repair_templates: Identify a codomain basis and verify openness of each preimage of a basic open set.

name: Pasting lemma for closed cover
statement: If X is the union of finitely many closed sets and a function is continuous on each piece with compatible values, then the function is continuous on X.
conditions: Each A_i is closed in X.
conclusion: f is continuous on X.
typical_uses: Prove continuity of piecewise-defined maps.
Repair piecewise-continuity proofs by adding closed-cover and agreement conditions.
common_misuses: Using infinitely many closed pieces without local finiteness or another theorem.
Ignoring agreement on overlaps for a piecewise definition.
bridge_lemmas: For closed C in Y, f^{-1}(C) is the finite union of closed sets A_i cap (f|A_i)^{-1}(C).
repair_templates: Verify each piece is closed in X and that formulas define the same value on overlaps.

name: Composition of continuous maps
statement: The composition of continuous maps is continuous.
conclusion: g o f:X->Z is continuous.
typical_uses: Build continuity of complex maps from simpler maps.
Repair a proof by inserting continuity of intermediate maps and domain-codomain matching.
common_misuses: Composing maps whose codomain and domain do not match.
Using continuity of g o f to infer continuity of f or g without extra assumptions.
repair_templates: Check the intermediate space and write the inverse-image equality before applying continuity twice.

name: Homeomorphism
statement: A homeomorphism is a bijective continuous map whose inverse is continuous.
conditions: X and Y are topological spaces.
conclusion: f is a homeomorphism and X and Y are topologically equivalent.
typical_uses: Transfer topological properties between spaces.
Repair arguments that prove only bijective continuity.
common_misuses: Assuming every continuous bijection is a homeomorphism.
Forgetting to prove continuity of the inverse or use a theorem that supplies it.
bridge_lemmas: A bijection is a homeomorphism iff it maps open sets of X to open sets of Y and has continuous inverse.
repair_templates: After proving continuous bijection, add compact-to-Hausdorff or open-map hypotheses, or directly prove inverse continuity.

name: Product topology on arbitrary products
statement: The product topology on prod X_alpha has as a basis the sets prod U_alpha where each U_alpha is open in X_alpha and U_alpha=X_alpha for all but finitely many indices.
conditions: {X_alpha} is an indexed family of topological spaces.
U_alpha is open in X_alpha for each alpha.
U_alpha=X_alpha except for finitely many alpha.
conclusion: Products prod U_alpha form a basis for the product topology.
typical_uses: Handle neighborhoods in infinite products.
Repair proofs that use box-open sets in the product topology.
common_misuses: Allowing infinitely many coordinates to be restricted and calling the set product-open.
Confusing product topology with box topology.
bridge_lemmas: A basic product neighborhood restricts only finitely many coordinates.
repair_templates: Replace infinitely many coordinate restrictions by finitely many restrictions, or explicitly switch to the box topology.

name: Projection maps are continuous
statement: Each coordinate projection from a product space with the product topology to a factor space is continuous.
conditions: X=prod X_alpha has the product topology.
conclusion: pi_beta is continuous.
typical_uses: Prove continuity of coordinate functions and maps into products.
Repair product topology arguments by using subbasic preimages.
common_misuses: Assuming projections from the box topology have all product-topology universal properties.
Confusing projection images with inverse images.
bridge_lemmas: pi_beta^{-1}(U)=U times the full product of all other factors, a subbasic open set.
repair_templates: Show continuity by computing the preimage of an open set in the target factor.

name: Continuity into a product by coordinates
statement: A map f:A->prod X_alpha is continuous for the product topology iff every coordinate map pi_alpha o f is continuous.
conditions: prod X_alpha has the product topology.
conclusion: f is continuous iff each coordinate function pi_alpha o f:A->X_alpha is continuous.
typical_uses: Reduce continuity into a product to coordinate continuity.
Repair a proof that checks coordinate maps but has not specified the product topology.
common_misuses: Using this criterion for the box topology without additional hypotheses.
Checking only finitely many coordinates when the product has infinitely many nontrivial coordinates.
bridge_lemmas: Subbasic open sets in the product are inverse images under projections.
repair_templates: State that the codomain has the product topology and verify all coordinate maps.

name: Metric topology from balls
statement: A metric d on X generates a topology whose basis consists of open balls B_d(x,epsilon) with epsilon>0.
conditions: d is a metric on X.
conclusion: The open balls form a basis for the metric topology on X.
typical_uses: Convert metric inequalities into open-neighborhood arguments.
Repair topological proofs in metric spaces by using balls as basis elements.
common_misuses: Using closed balls as the basis without proof.
Forgetting epsilon must be positive.
bridge_lemmas: If y is in B(x,epsilon), choose delta=epsilon-d(x,y)>0 so B(y,delta) subset B(x,epsilon).
repair_templates: Given a point in an open ball, shrink the radius using the triangle inequality.

name: Metric epsilon-delta continuity
statement: For maps between metric spaces, topological continuity at a point is equivalent to the epsilon-delta condition.
conclusion: f is continuous at a iff for every epsilon>0 there exists delta>0 such that d_X(x,a)<delta implies d_Y(f(x),f(a))<epsilon.
typical_uses: Translate between topological continuity and metric estimates.
Repair a metric proof by making the dependence of delta on epsilon and a explicit.
common_misuses: Choosing delta depending on x instead of epsilon and a.
Using a metric not associated with the stated topology.
bridge_lemmas: Open balls form bases for metric topologies.
repair_templates: Fix epsilon first, choose delta before x is specialized, and prove the implication for all x in the delta-ball.

name: Convergence in metric spaces
statement: A sequence x_n in a metric space converges to x iff for every epsilon>0, eventually d(x_n,x)<epsilon.
conclusion: x_n converges to x iff for every epsilon>0 there exists N such that n>=N implies d(x_n,x)<epsilon.
typical_uses: Check sequence limits in metric-topology proofs.
Repair a sequence argument by adding the eventual quantifier.
common_misuses: Using sequences to characterize closure in arbitrary non-first-countable spaces.
Letting N depend on n.
bridge_lemmas: Metric open balls form a neighborhood basis at each point.
repair_templates: State the epsilon and eventual-N quantifiers explicitly and restrict sequence arguments to metric or first-countable spaces.

name: Uniform limit theorem
statement: A uniform limit of continuous maps into a metric space is continuous.
conditions: f_n:X->Y is continuous for every n.
conclusion: f is continuous.
typical_uses: Repair a limit-of-functions proof by strengthening pointwise convergence to uniform convergence.
Check continuity claims for limits of continuous functions.
common_misuses: Using pointwise convergence as if it implied continuity of the limit.
Omitting the metric structure on the codomain for uniform convergence.
bridge_lemmas: Use the triangle inequality with epsilon/3 and choose one continuous f_N uniformly close to f.
repair_templates: Add a uniform convergence hypothesis or provide a separate continuity proof for the limit.

name: Quotient topology
statement: For a surjective map p:X->Y, the quotient topology on Y declares U open exactly when p^{-1}(U) is open in X.
conclusion: The family of subsets U of Y with p^{-1}(U) open in X is a topology on Y, called the quotient topology.
typical_uses: Analyze spaces formed by identifications.
Repair quotient arguments by checking openness through the projection preimage.
common_misuses: Forgetting p must be surjective for the usual quotient-map setup.
Assuming U is open in Y because p^{-1}(U) is saturated but not open.
bridge_lemmas: Preimages preserve arbitrary unions and finite intersections.
repair_templates: Prove p^{-1}(U) is open in X, and verify the subset U of Y is well-defined under the identification.

name: Map out of quotient criterion
statement: If p:X->Y is a quotient map, then g:Y->Z is continuous iff g o p:X->Z is continuous.
conclusion: g is continuous iff g o p is continuous.
typical_uses: Define continuous maps from quotient spaces by checking the composite on the original space.
Repair quotient proofs that check the wrong map.
common_misuses: Applying the criterion to a surjection not known to be quotient.
Defining g on equivalence classes without proving it is well-defined.
bridge_lemmas: g^{-1}(V) is open in Y iff p^{-1}(g^{-1}(V))=(g o p)^{-1}(V) is open in X.
repair_templates: First prove p is quotient and g is well-defined, then check continuity of g o p.

name: Connected space
statement: A space is connected when it cannot be written as the union of two disjoint nonempty separated open subsets.
conclusion: X is connected iff there do not exist nonempty disjoint open sets U,V in X with X=U union V.
typical_uses: Prove connectedness by ruling out separations.
Repair arguments that use a separation without proving both sets are open in the subspace.
common_misuses: Allowing one side of a separation to be empty.
Using open in the ambient space instead of open in X.
bridge_lemmas: A separation can equivalently be given by a nonempty proper subset that is both open and closed in X.
repair_templates: Show the alleged separating sets are nonempty, disjoint, cover X, and are open in the relevant subspace.

name: Connected iff only trivial clopen sets
statement: A topological space is connected iff its only subsets that are both open and closed are the empty set and the whole space.
conclusion: X is connected iff every clopen subset of X is either empty or X.
typical_uses: Prove connectedness by excluding nontrivial clopen subsets.
Detect invalid connectedness claims from existence of a nontrivial clopen set.
common_misuses: Checking clopen subsets in an ambient space rather than in X.
Forgetting that empty set and X are always clopen.
bridge_lemmas: A nontrivial clopen subset A gives the separation A and X\A.
repair_templates: Convert the claimed separation into a nontrivial clopen set, or prove every clopen subset is trivial.

name: Continuous image of connected space
statement: The image of a connected space under a continuous map is connected.
conclusion: f(X) is connected as a subspace of Y.
typical_uses: Transfer connectedness through continuous maps.
Repair a proof that tries to use connectedness of the codomain instead of the image.
common_misuses: Omitting continuity of f.
Concluding Y is connected when f is not surjective.
bridge_lemmas: A separation of f(X) pulls back to a separation of X if both sides meet the image.
repair_templates: Add surjectivity if the goal is connectedness of all of Y; otherwise conclude only f(X) is connected.

name: Union of connected subspaces with common point
statement: A union of connected subspaces with a common point is connected.
conditions: {A_i} is a family of connected subspaces of X.
There exists p in X such that p belongs to A_i for every i.
conclusion: Union_i A_i is connected.
typical_uses: Build connected sets from overlapping connected pieces.
Repair connectedness proofs by identifying a common intersection point.
common_misuses: Using pairwise disjoint connected pieces and concluding their union is connected.
Forgetting the subspace topology on each A_i.
bridge_lemmas: If a separation of the union existed, each connected A_i would lie entirely in one side, and the common point forces the same side.
repair_templates: Prove all pieces meet a fixed connected core or common point before invoking the union rule.

name: Closure of connected set
statement: If A is connected, then any set B with A subset B subset cl(A) is connected; in particular cl(A) is connected.
conditions: A is a connected subspace of X.
B is a subset of X.
conclusion: B is connected.
typical_uses: Extend connectedness from a dense connected subset to its closure.
Repair proofs about intervals with endpoints added.
common_misuses: Assuming every superset of a connected set is connected.
Using closure in the wrong ambient space.
bridge_lemmas: A separation of B would separate A, and each side closed in B would conflict with B subset cl(A).
repair_templates: Show the added points lie in the closure of the original connected set before applying the closure rule.

name: Intermediate value property from connectedness
statement: A continuous real-valued map on a connected space has interval image and hence takes every intermediate value.
conditions: r lies between f(a) and f(b).
conclusion: There exists c in X such that f(c)=r.
typical_uses: Prove existence of roots or intermediate values using connectedness.
Repair IVT arguments by adding connectedness of the domain and continuity.
common_misuses: Applying IVT on a disconnected domain.
Assuming the codomain order result applies to non-ordered spaces.
bridge_lemmas: Connected subspaces of R are intervals.
repair_templates: Restrict to a connected subspace containing the two points, or prove the relevant subset is connected.

name: Connected subsets of the real line
statement: A subset of R with the usual topology is connected exactly when it is an interval, including possibly a point or empty set depending on convention.
conditions: A is a subset of R with the subspace topology.
conclusion: A is connected iff whenever x<z<y with x,y in A, then z in A.
typical_uses: Classify connected subsets of R.
Repair a proof by checking the order-convex interval property.
common_misuses: Calling a union of separated intervals connected.
Forgetting singleton intervals are connected.
bridge_lemmas: If A omits z between x and y, then A cap (-infinity,z) and A cap (z,infinity) separate A.
repair_templates: Show the subset contains every real number between any two of its points.

name: Path connected implies connected
statement: Every path-connected topological space is connected.
conditions: X is path connected: for any x,y in X there is a continuous path gamma:[0,1]->X from x to y.
conclusion: X is connected.
typical_uses: Prove connectedness by constructing paths.
Repair a connectedness proof that only establishes paths between points in one component.
common_misuses: Assuming connected implies path connected in arbitrary spaces.
Forgetting path continuity.
bridge_lemmas: The interval [0,1] is connected and continuous images of connected sets are connected.
repair_templates: If path connectedness fails, use another connectedness criterion instead of reversing the implication.

name: Components are maximal connected subspaces
statement: A component of X is a maximal connected subset of X; components partition X and are closed in X.
conclusion: Every point of X lies in a unique component, components are pairwise disjoint, and each component is closed.
typical_uses: Localize connectedness arguments to components.
Repair claims that components overlap without being equal.
common_misuses: Assuming components are always open.
Confusing path components with components.
bridge_lemmas: The union of all connected subsets containing a fixed point is connected and maximal.
repair_templates: Prove openness of components only under extra hypotheses such as local connectedness.

name: Components of open sets in locally connected spaces
statement: A space is locally connected iff components of open subsets are open.
conclusion: X is locally connected iff for every open U subset X, each component of U is open in X.
typical_uses: Prove local connectedness or openness of components.
Repair arguments that treat components of open sets as open without local connectedness.
common_misuses: Assuming components of every space are open.
Using path components where connected components are meant.
bridge_lemmas: Local connectedness gives connected open neighborhoods inside any open neighborhood.
repair_templates: Add local connectedness or prove directly that the relevant component is open.

name: Compactness by open covers
statement: A space X is compact if every open cover of X has a finite subcover.
conditions: Every cover of X by open subsets of X has a finite subcollection still covering X.
conclusion: X is compact.
typical_uses: Prove compactness directly or check compactness-preserving theorems.
Repair compactness arguments by verifying the cover is open and covers the whole space.
common_misuses: Using finite subcover for one particular cover as proof of compactness.
Using sets open in a larger space without checking relative openness.
bridge_lemmas: For a subspace A, an open cover of A uses sets open in A, equivalently intersections with ambient open sets.
repair_templates: Start with an arbitrary open cover and derive a finite subcover, keeping the ambient space explicit.

name: Closed subspace of compact space
statement: A closed subset of a compact space is compact.
conclusion: A is compact as a subspace.
typical_uses: Prove compactness of subsets using ambient compactness.
Repair compactness claims by adding closedness of the subset.
common_misuses: Assuming every subset of a compact space is compact.
Using closedness in a different ambient space.
bridge_lemmas: Given an open cover of A, add X\A to cover X and take a finite subcover.
repair_templates: Show A is closed in the compact ambient space before invoking compactness inheritance.

name: Compact subsets of Hausdorff spaces are closed
statement: Every compact subspace of a Hausdorff space is closed.
conditions: A is a compact subset of X.
conclusion: A is closed in X.
typical_uses: Prove closedness from compactness in Hausdorff spaces.
Repair arguments that omit the Hausdorff assumption.
common_misuses: Claiming compact subsets are closed in arbitrary topological spaces.
Using compactness of X instead of compactness of A.
bridge_lemmas: For x outside A, separate x from each a in A by disjoint neighborhoods and use a finite subcover of A.
repair_templates: Add Hausdorffness of the ambient space or prove closedness by another method.

name: Continuous image of compact space
statement: The image of a compact space under a continuous map is compact.
conclusion: f(X) is compact in Y.
typical_uses: Prove compactness of images and ranges.
Repair proof steps that transfer compactness through maps.
common_misuses: Applying the theorem without continuity.
Assuming inverse images of compact sets are compact without extra hypotheses.
bridge_lemmas: Pull back an open cover of f(X) along f to obtain an open cover of X.
repair_templates: Add continuity of f and apply compactness to the pulled-back cover.

name: Continuous bijection from compact to Hausdorff
statement: A continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism.
conclusion: f is a homeomorphism.
typical_uses: Avoid separately proving inverse continuity.
Repair false homeomorphism proofs by adding compact-Hausdorff hypotheses.
common_misuses: Dropping compactness of the domain or Hausdorffness of the codomain.
Assuming any continuous bijection is a homeomorphism.
bridge_lemmas: Closed subsets of X are compact, continuous images of them are compact, and compact subsets of Y are closed.
repair_templates: After proving continuous bijection, verify compact domain and Hausdorff codomain before concluding homeomorphism.

name: Finite product of compact spaces
statement: The product of finitely many compact spaces is compact.
conditions: X_1 x ... x X_n has the product topology.
conclusion: X_1 x ... x X_n is compact.
typical_uses: Prove compactness of rectangles and finite product spaces.
Repair product compactness arguments that do not specify the product topology.
common_misuses: Extending the finite result to arbitrary products without invoking Tychonoff.
Using the box topology for an infinite product.
bridge_lemmas: The tube lemma is commonly used for the two-factor case.
repair_templates: For infinitely many factors, cite Tychonoff with choice assumptions; for finite products, reduce inductively using the two-factor theorem.

name: Tube lemma
statement: If Y is compact and N is open in X x Y containing {x0} x Y, then some neighborhood W of x0 satisfies W x Y subset N.
conditions: N is open in X x Y.
conclusion: There is an open neighborhood W of x0 in X such that W x Y subset N.
typical_uses: Prove product compactness and local uniform containment in products.
Repair product-neighborhood arguments requiring one uniform neighborhood over a compact factor.
common_misuses: Using the lemma when the fiber factor is not compact.
Assuming the same tube exists for all x without proof.
bridge_lemmas: Cover {x0} x Y by finitely many product neighborhoods whose Y-parts cover Y, then intersect the X-parts.
repair_templates: Verify compactness of the fiber factor and construct a finite subcover before choosing W.

name: Heine-Borel theorem for real line
statement: A subset of R^n with the usual topology is compact iff it is closed and bounded.
conditions: A is a subset of R^n with the standard Euclidean topology.
conclusion: A is compact iff A is closed and bounded.
typical_uses: Prove compactness of concrete Euclidean sets.
Repair compactness claims in R^n by checking both closedness and boundedness.
common_misuses: Applying closed and bounded iff compact outside Euclidean finite-dimensional spaces.
Forgetting boundedness or closedness.
bridge_lemmas: Closed subspaces of compact boxes are compact; compact subsets of Hausdorff spaces are closed and projections or coordinate bounds give boundedness.
repair_templates: If outside R^n, replace Heine-Borel with the appropriate compactness theorem or prove compactness by open covers.

name: Extreme value theorem
statement: A continuous real-valued function on a compact space attains a maximum and a minimum.
conclusion: There exist x_min,x_max in X such that f(x_min)<=f(x)<=f(x_max) for all x in X.
typical_uses: Prove existence of extrema without computing them.
Repair optimization proofs by adding compactness and continuity.
common_misuses: Using the theorem on noncompact domains.
Using it for discontinuous functions.
bridge_lemmas: f(X) is compact in R, hence closed and bounded and contains its infimum and supremum.
repair_templates: Show the domain is compact and f is continuous, or restrict to a compact subspace where extrema are sought.

name: Lebesgue number lemma
statement: Every open cover of a compact metric space has a positive Lebesgue number.
conditions: A is an open cover of X.
conclusion: There exists delta>0 such that every subset of X with diameter less than delta is contained in some member of the cover.
typical_uses: Turn open-cover information into uniform metric estimates.
Repair arguments that need a uniform local scale over a compact space.
common_misuses: Using a Lebesgue number without compactness.
Applying the lemma in a non-metric space without a metric formulation.
bridge_lemmas: For each point choose a ball contained in a cover element and use compactness to make the radii uniform.
repair_templates: Add compact metric hypotheses, or replace the uniform delta claim with a pointwise neighborhood argument.

name: Continuity on compact metric space is uniform
statement: A continuous map from a compact metric space to a metric space is uniformly continuous.
conclusion: For every epsilon>0 there exists delta>0 such that d_X(x,y)<delta implies d_Y(f(x),f(y))<epsilon for all x,y in X.
typical_uses: Promote pointwise continuity to uniform estimates on compact domains.
Repair epsilon-delta proofs that need a single delta for all points.
common_misuses: Assuming continuity implies uniform continuity on noncompact domains.
Choosing delta depending on x in a uniform-continuity proof.
bridge_lemmas: Use a Lebesgue number for the cover by continuity neighborhoods.
repair_templates: Verify compactness of the domain or restrict to a compact subset before asserting uniform continuity.

name: Limit point compactness
statement: A space is limit point compact if every infinite subset has a limit point in the space.
conclusion: X is limit point compact iff every infinite A subset X has some limit point x in X.
typical_uses: Analyze weaker compactness properties and counterexamples.
Repair arguments that confuse compactness with limit point compactness.
common_misuses: Assuming limit point compactness is equivalent to compactness in every space.
Allowing the limit point to lie outside X.
bridge_lemmas: In metric spaces, compactness, sequential compactness, and limit point compactness are closely related under standard hypotheses.
repair_templates: If using equivalence with compactness, add metric or second-countable conditions as required by the theorem being invoked.

name: Metric compactness and sequential compactness
statement: For metric spaces, compactness is equivalent to sequential compactness.
conclusion: X is compact iff every sequence in X has a convergent subsequence with limit in X.
typical_uses: Prove compactness or noncompactness in metric spaces using sequences.
Repair sequential arguments by adding the metric-space hypothesis.
common_misuses: Using sequential compactness as equivalent to compactness in arbitrary topological spaces.
Letting the subsequence converge outside the space.
bridge_lemmas: Compact metric spaces are limit point compact and have finite epsilon-nets; sequential compactness gives open-cover compactness.
repair_templates: State that X is metric before replacing open-cover compactness with subsequence compactness.

name: Local compactness
statement: A space is locally compact at x if x has a neighborhood contained in a compact subspace; it is locally compact if this holds at every point.
conclusion: X is locally compact at x iff there is an open neighborhood U of x and compact C subset X with U subset C.
typical_uses: Check hypotheses for one-point compactification and local compactness arguments.
Repair local compactness claims by producing compact neighborhoods.
common_misuses: Confusing local compactness with every open neighborhood being compact.
Using compact closure without proving it is compact.
bridge_lemmas: In Hausdorff spaces, compact neighborhoods can often be taken with open U whose closure is compact.
repair_templates: Find one sufficiently small neighborhood with compact closure, rather than trying to make every neighborhood compact.

name: One-point compactification of locally compact Hausdorff space
statement: A noncompact locally compact Hausdorff space has a one-point compactification whose neighborhoods of the new point are complements of compact closed subsets, and the result is compact Hausdorff.
conclusion: There is a compact Hausdorff space X* = X union {infty} containing X densely, with neighborhoods of infty of the form X*\C where C is compact closed in X.
typical_uses: Construct compactifications and analyze behavior at infinity.
Repair one-point compactification arguments by checking local compactness and Hausdorffness.
common_misuses: Applying the construction to spaces that are not locally compact Hausdorff.
Using arbitrary closed sets instead of compact closed sets for neighborhoods of infinity.
bridge_lemmas: Compact subsets of Hausdorff spaces are closed; local compactness separates a point from infinity by compact neighborhoods.
repair_templates: Verify X is locally compact Hausdorff and noncompact before using the standard neighborhood basis at infinity.

name: First countability
statement: A space is first countable if each point has a countable neighborhood basis.
conclusion: X is first countable iff for each x in X there is a countable collection of neighborhoods of x such that every neighborhood of x contains one of them.
typical_uses: Justify sequence-based closure and continuity arguments.
Repair proofs that use sequences in spaces where first countability has not been shown.
common_misuses: Assuming all topological spaces are first countable.
Confusing first countability with second countability.
bridge_lemmas: Metric spaces are first countable using balls of radius 1/n.
repair_templates: Add a countable local basis at the relevant point before using sequences to capture closure.

name: Closure by sequences in first-countable spaces
statement: In a first-countable space, x lies in the closure of A iff some sequence of points of A converges to x.
conditions: A is a subset of X.
conclusion: x in cl(A) iff there exists a sequence a_n in A converging to x.
typical_uses: Use sequences to prove closure membership when first countability is available.
Repair non-sequential closure arguments by adding first-countability or switching to neighborhoods.
common_misuses: Applying the sequential criterion in arbitrary spaces.
Forgetting the sequence terms must lie in A.
bridge_lemmas: Choose a nested countable local basis at x and pick a_n in A from each basis neighborhood.
repair_templates: If first countability is absent, replace the sequence proof with the neighborhood criterion for closure.

name: Second countability implies Lindelof and separable
statement: Every second-countable space is Lindelof and separable.
conclusion: Every open cover of X has a countable subcover, and X has a countable dense subset.
typical_uses: Derive countable subcovers or dense sets from a countable basis.
Repair proofs that assume separability implies second countability without extra metric hypotheses.
common_misuses: Reversing the implication in arbitrary spaces.
Confusing countable cover with finite subcover.
bridge_lemmas: Choose one basis element contained in a cover member for each covered point; select one point from each nonempty basis element for density.
repair_templates: Use the countable basis to construct the needed countable subcover or countable dense subset explicitly.

name: Separable metric spaces are second countable
statement: In metric spaces, separability implies second countability.
conditions: D is a countable dense subset of X.
conclusion: The balls with centers in D and positive rational radii form a countable basis for X.
typical_uses: Move from separability to basis arguments in metric spaces.
Repair a proof that uses this implication outside metric spaces.
common_misuses: Claiming separability implies second countability for all topological spaces.
Using arbitrary real radii and losing countability.
bridge_lemmas: Density lets each ball around x contain a center d in D with a smaller rational radius ball around d contained in the original ball.
repair_templates: Restrict to rational radii and dense-set centers, and cite the metric triangle inequality for refinement.

name: Hausdorff space
statement: A space is Hausdorff if any two distinct points have disjoint open neighborhoods.
conclusion: X is Hausdorff iff for all x!=y in X, there exist open U,V with x in U, y in V, and U cap V empty.
typical_uses: Separate points and prove uniqueness of limits.
Repair compactness-to-closedness arguments by supplying the Hausdorff hypothesis.
common_misuses: Using Hausdorff separation for arbitrary closed sets instead of points.
Assuming every topology is Hausdorff.
bridge_lemmas: In a Hausdorff space, compact subsets are closed and limits of sequences or nets are unique under appropriate convergence notions.
repair_templates: When separating more than points, check whether regularity or normality is the needed stronger axiom.

name: Regular and normal spaces
statement: A regular space separates points from closed sets by disjoint neighborhoods; a normal space separates disjoint closed sets by disjoint neighborhoods, with standard T1 assumptions in Munkres conventions.
conditions: X is a T1 topological space for the standard named axioms.
conclusion: X is regular if points and disjoint closed sets can be separated; X is normal if disjoint closed sets can be separated by disjoint open neighborhoods.
typical_uses: Identify which separation axiom is needed for shrinking neighborhoods or Urysohn-type results.
Repair proofs that use normality while only Hausdorffness is known.
common_misuses: Confusing Hausdorff, regular, and normal separation strengths.
Omitting T1 assumptions when using named versions.
bridge_lemmas: Normal implies regular under T1 conventions; regular plus suitable bases can yield neighborhood closure refinements.
repair_templates: State the exact separation axiom being used and verify its hypotheses before separating a point from a closed set or two closed sets.

name: T1 iff singletons are closed
statement: A space is T1 exactly when every singleton subset is closed.
conclusion: X is T1 iff {x} is closed in X for every x in X.
typical_uses: Convert T1 assumptions into closedness of finite sets.
Repair separation proofs that need singleton closedness.
common_misuses: Assuming Hausdorff is needed merely to show singletons are closed.
Using T1 to separate points by disjoint neighborhoods, which requires Hausdorff.
bridge_lemmas: Finite unions of closed singleton sets are closed.
repair_templates: Use T1 to show finite sets are closed, but add Hausdorff if disjoint neighborhoods of two points are required.

name: Regular neighborhood shrinking
statement: In a regular space, if U is an open neighborhood of x, then there is an open V with x in V and cl(V) subset U.
conditions: X is regular with the standard T1 convention.
conclusion: There exists open V such that x in V and cl_X(V) subset U.
typical_uses: Shrink neighborhoods while controlling closures.
Repair proofs that need closure containment rather than just set containment.
common_misuses: Using closure shrinking in spaces not known to be regular.
Concluding cl(U) subset U for arbitrary open U.
bridge_lemmas: Separate x from the closed set X\U by disjoint open neighborhoods.
repair_templates: Invoke regularity on x and X\U, then take the neighborhood whose closure avoids X\U.

name: Normal closed-set shrinking
statement: In a normal space, if A is closed and U is open with A subset U, then there is open V with A subset V and cl(V) subset U.
conclusion: There exists open V with A subset V and cl_X(V) subset U.
typical_uses: Prepare nested open sets for Urysohn lemma and extension arguments.
Repair proofs that need an open set whose closure remains inside a prescribed open set.
common_misuses: Applying normal shrinking when A is not closed.
Using regularity for two closed sets when normality is needed.
bridge_lemmas: Separate the disjoint closed sets A and X\U by open neighborhoods.
repair_templates: First prove A is closed and X\U is closed, then apply normality to separate them.

name: Metric spaces are normal
statement: Every metric space is normal.
conditions: X is a metric space with its metric topology.
conclusion: X is normal.
typical_uses: Use Urysohn or Tietze-type results in metric spaces.
Repair a normality proof by constructing distance neighborhoods.
common_misuses: Assuming every Hausdorff space is normal.
Using a distance-to-set argument without a metric.
bridge_lemmas: For disjoint closed A and B, the functions d(x,A) and d(x,B) give disjoint open neighborhoods.
repair_templates: When normality is needed, either cite metric normality or explicitly define separated neighborhoods by distance to closed sets.

name: Compact Hausdorff spaces are normal
statement: Every compact Hausdorff space is normal.
conclusion: X is normal.
typical_uses: Apply normal-space theorems to compact Hausdorff spaces.
Repair proofs that need normality from compactness plus Hausdorffness.
common_misuses: Claiming compact alone implies normal.
Claiming Hausdorff alone implies normal.
bridge_lemmas: Compact subsets of Hausdorff spaces are closed, and finite subcovers combine pointwise Hausdorff separations.
repair_templates: Verify both compactness and Hausdorffness before invoking normality.

name: Urysohn lemma
statement: In a normal space, two disjoint closed sets can be separated by a continuous function to [0,1] taking values 0 and 1 on the two sets.
conditions: A and B are disjoint closed subsets of X.
conclusion: There exists continuous f:X->[0,1] such that f(A)={0} and f(B)={1}.
typical_uses: Construct continuous functions with prescribed values on closed sets.
Repair separation arguments that require functional rather than open-set separation.
common_misuses: Using Urysohn lemma in spaces not known to be normal.
Trying to prescribe arbitrary values on nonclosed sets.
bridge_lemmas: Normal closed-set shrinking constructs nested open sets indexed by rationals.
repair_templates: Check A and B are closed and disjoint, prove normality, then apply Urysohn instead of handwaving a separating function.

name: Urysohn metrization theorem
statement: Every regular second-countable T1 space is metrizable.
conditions: X is T1 under the standard convention.
conclusion: There exists a metric on X inducing its topology.
typical_uses: Prove metrizability from separation and countability hypotheses.
Repair metrizability claims by checking second countability and regularity.
common_misuses: Replacing second countability with separability in non-metric settings.
Omitting regularity or T1 assumptions.
bridge_lemmas: Use countably many Urysohn functions to embed X into a countable product of intervals.
repair_templates: Verify a countable basis and regular T1 separation before citing the metrization theorem.

name: Tietze extension theorem
statement: A continuous bounded real-valued function on a closed subset of a normal space extends continuously to the whole space.
conditions: f is bounded, or equivalently has image in a closed interval for the common bounded form.
conclusion: There exists continuous F:X->R extending f; in the interval-valued form F may be chosen with the same interval bounds.
typical_uses: Extend functions from closed subspaces.
Repair extension claims by adding normality, closed domain, and bounded or interval-valued hypotheses.
common_misuses: Extending from a nonclosed subset without extra conditions.
Applying the bounded version to an unbounded function without citing the unbounded variant.
bridge_lemmas: Urysohn lemma supplies successive approximations for extension.
repair_templates: First show the subset is closed in a normal space and that the target bounds match the theorem version being used.

name: Tychonoff theorem
statement: An arbitrary product of compact spaces is compact in the product topology.
conditions: {X_alpha} is a family of compact topological spaces.
prod X_alpha has the product topology.
conclusion: prod X_alpha is compact.
typical_uses: Prove compactness of infinite products.
Repair arguments that incorrectly use finite-product compactness for arbitrary products.
common_misuses: Using the box topology instead of the product topology.
Ignoring the set-theoretic choice principle often underlying the theorem.
bridge_lemmas: The product topology has subbasic sets from coordinate projections; Alexander subbase theorem is a common proof route.
repair_templates: State the topology is the product topology and cite Tychonoff rather than finite-product induction.

name: Alexander subbase theorem
statement: A space with subbasis S is compact if every cover by subbasic open sets has a finite subcover.
conditions: S is a subbasis for X.
Every cover of X by elements of S has a finite subcover.
conclusion: X is compact.
typical_uses: Prove compactness from subbasic covers, especially in products.
Repair compactness proofs that check only a basis or subbasis without a valid theorem.
common_misuses: Assuming arbitrary subbasic cover checks suffice without invoking Alexander's theorem.
Confusing subbasic covers with arbitrary open covers without the theorem.
bridge_lemmas: The theorem is commonly proved using maximal open covers and choice/Zorn-type arguments.
repair_templates: Explicitly cite Alexander subbase theorem when reducing compactness to subbasic open covers.

name: Inverse images preserve set operations
statement: For a function f:X->Y, inverse images preserve unions, intersections, and complements exactly.
conditions: {B_i} is a family of subsets of Y.
conclusion: f^{-1}(union B_i)=union f^{-1}(B_i), f^{-1}(intersection B_i)=intersection f^{-1}(B_i), and f^{-1}(Y\B)=X\f^{-1}(B).
typical_uses: Justify continuity proofs based on open or closed preimages.
Repair arguments that incorrectly use direct images where inverse images are needed.
common_misuses: Assuming direct images preserve intersections or complements without extra hypotheses.
Forgetting the complement in the domain is relative to X.
bridge_lemmas: Membership in f^{-1}(B) means f(x) belongs to B.
repair_templates: Rewrite the disputed step pointwise using membership, then apply the exact inverse-image identity.

name: Direct images preserve unions but not intersections generally
statement: For a function f, direct images preserve arbitrary unions, while f(A cap B) is always contained in f(A) cap f(B) and equality may require injectivity on the relevant sets.
conditions: {A_i} is a family of subsets of X.
conclusion: f(union A_i)=union f(A_i), and f(A cap B) subset f(A) cap f(B).
typical_uses: Detect invalid image-intersection steps in topology proofs.
Repair calculations involving images of unions and intersections.
common_misuses: Replacing f(A cap B) by f(A) cap f(B) without injectivity.
Assuming images preserve complements.
bridge_lemmas: If f is injective on A union B, then f(A cap B)=f(A) cap f(B).
repair_templates: Use only the inclusion, or add an injectivity hypothesis before claiming equality.

name: Equivalence relations and partitions
statement: An equivalence relation on X determines a partition into equivalence classes, and every partition determines an equivalence relation.
conditions: ~ is an equivalence relation on X.
conclusion: The equivalence classes [x] are nonempty, pairwise disjoint or equal, and their union is X.
typical_uses: Check quotient-space constructions and well-defined maps on classes.
Repair proofs that use representatives without proving independence of representative.
common_misuses: Treating overlapping equivalence classes as distinct.
Defining a quotient map without verifying the relation is an equivalence relation.
bridge_lemmas: [x]=[y] iff x~y.
repair_templates: Before defining a function on X/~, prove that equivalent representatives give the same output.

name: Choice function for nonempty family
statement: The axiom of choice permits selecting one element from each set in a family of nonempty sets.
conditions: {A_i} is an indexed family of nonempty sets.
conclusion: There exists a function c with c(i) in A_i for every index i.
typical_uses: Justify constructions choosing representatives, basis elements, or local data from infinitely many nonempty sets.
Repair proofs with hidden infinite choices.
common_misuses: Using a simultaneous arbitrary choice from possibly empty sets.
Forgetting that finite choice needs no full axiom of choice.
bridge_lemmas: A product of nonempty sets is nonempty under the axiom of choice.
repair_templates: Verify each set being chosen from is nonempty, then state the choice principle being used.

name: Well-ordering principle
statement: Every set can be given a well-order, assuming the standard choice principle equivalences.
conditions: The well-ordering principle or an equivalent form of choice is available.
conclusion: There is a linear order on A in which every nonempty subset has a least element.
typical_uses: Support transfinite constructions and maximality arguments.
Repair proofs that require choosing least counterexamples in arbitrary sets.
common_misuses: Assuming a natural well-order exists without specifying one.
Using well-order induction on a relation not known to be a well-order.
bridge_lemmas: Transfinite induction applies to well-ordered sets.
repair_templates: Introduce an explicit well-order or replace the argument with Zorn's lemma when maximal objects are needed.

name: Maximal principle
statement: If every chain in a partially ordered set has an upper bound, then the poset has a maximal element.
conditions: P is a nonempty partially ordered set.
Every chain in P has an upper bound in P.
The maximal principle or an equivalent choice principle is available.
conclusion: P contains a maximal element.
typical_uses: Prove existence of maximal covers, bases, ideals, extensions, or lifting domains.
Repair maximality arguments by checking chain upper bounds.
common_misuses: Checking upper bounds only for finite chains.
Confusing maximal with maximum.
bridge_lemmas: The union of a chain is often the upper bound in inclusion-ordered families, but it must remain in P.
repair_templates: Define the poset precisely and prove that the chain union or candidate upper bound satisfies all defining conditions.

name: Box topology basis
statement: The box topology on a product has basis all products of open sets in the factors, allowing restrictions in every coordinate.
conditions: {X_alpha} is an indexed family of topological spaces.
U_alpha is open in X_alpha for every alpha.
conclusion: Sets of the form prod U_alpha form a basis for the box topology.
typical_uses: Distinguish box topology from product topology in infinite products.
Repair proofs that use infinitely many coordinate restrictions.
common_misuses: Calling an infinite-coordinate box basic open in the product topology.
Using product-topology continuity criteria for box topology.
bridge_lemmas: For finite products, box and product topologies agree.
repair_templates: If infinitely many coordinates are restricted, either switch to box topology or replace the set by product-basic neighborhoods with finitely many restrictions.

name: Open or closed surjection is quotient
statement: A continuous surjective map that is open or closed is a quotient map.
conditions: p is an open map or p is a closed map.
conclusion: Y has the quotient topology with respect to p, so U subset Y is open iff p^{-1}(U) is open in X.
typical_uses: Verify quotient-map hypotheses without checking the definition directly.
Repair quotient arguments by adding openness or closedness of the projection.
common_misuses: Assuming every continuous surjection is quotient.
Using an open-map argument for a map that only sends some basic opens to open sets without proof.
bridge_lemmas: If p is open and p^{-1}(U) is open, then U=p(p^{-1}(U)) is open.
repair_templates: Prove p is open or closed, or verify the quotient definition directly.

name: Translations in a topological group are homeomorphisms
statement: In a topological group, left and right translations and inversion are homeomorphisms.
conditions: a is an element of G.
conclusion: The maps x->ax, x->xa, and x->x^{-1} are homeomorphisms of G.
typical_uses: Move local topological arguments from the identity to arbitrary group elements.
Repair proofs by reducing neighborhood claims to neighborhoods of the identity.
common_misuses: Using group translations as homeomorphisms before proving the group operations are continuous.
Assuming a purely algebraic group has these topological properties.
bridge_lemmas: Translation inverse maps are translations by a^{-1}; inversion is its own inverse.
repair_templates: Verify the space is a topological group, then translate the neighborhood or closure statement to the identity.

name: Stone-Cech extension property
statement: For a completely regular space X, the Stone-Cech compactification beta X is compact Hausdorff and every continuous map from X to a compact Hausdorff space extends uniquely over beta X.
conditions: X is completely regular in the relevant convention.
beta X is the Stone-Cech compactification of X.
conclusion: There exists a unique continuous F:beta X->K extending f.
typical_uses: Repair extension arguments involving bounded continuous functions or compact targets.
Recognize the universal property characterizing beta X.
common_misuses: Applying the universal property to noncompact Hausdorff targets.
Omitting complete regularity or the compactification setup.
bridge_lemmas: Embedding X into a product of intervals by bounded continuous functions is a common construction.
repair_templates: Check the target is compact Hausdorff and the map is defined on X, then invoke the universal property.

name: Locally finite closures and unions
statement: For a locally finite family of subsets, taking closures preserves local finiteness and the closure of the union equals the union of closures under standard hypotheses.
conditions: {A_i} is a locally finite family of subsets of X.
conclusion: {cl(A_i)} is locally finite, and cl(union A_i)=union cl(A_i).
typical_uses: Control closures in paracompactness and partition-of-unity style arguments.
Repair invalid closure-of-infinite-union steps.
common_misuses: Assuming closure distributes over arbitrary unions without local finiteness.
Forgetting to prove local finiteness at every point.
bridge_lemmas: A neighborhood meeting only finitely many A_i also meets only finitely many cl(A_i) after shrinking or using the local finiteness argument.
repair_templates: Add local finiteness before replacing the closure of a union by the union of closures.

name: Nagata-Smirnov metrization theorem
statement: A regular space with a basis that is a countable union of locally finite families is metrizable.
conditions: X is regular with the standard separation convention.
X has a basis B such that B is the union of countably many locally finite collections.
conclusion: X is metrizable.
typical_uses: Prove metrizability using sigma-locally finite bases.
Repair metrizability claims that cite second countability when only a sigma-locally finite basis is available.
common_misuses: Omitting regularity.
Using point-finite instead of locally finite without an appropriate theorem.
bridge_lemmas: Locally finite basis refinements allow construction of separating continuous functions or metrics.
repair_templates: Show the proposed basis is both a basis and sigma-locally finite, and verify regularity.

name: Paracompact space
statement: A space is paracompact if every open cover has a locally finite open refinement that covers the space.
conclusion: X is paracompact iff every open cover of X admits a locally finite open refinement.
typical_uses: Check hypotheses for partitions of unity, normality, and metrization theorems.
Repair cover-refinement arguments by distinguishing refinement from subcover.
common_misuses: Confusing locally finite refinement with finite subcover.
Assuming every open cover itself is locally finite.
bridge_lemmas: A refinement cover has each refining set contained in some member of the original cover.
repair_templates: Given an open cover, construct or cite a locally finite open refinement and verify it still covers X.

name: Paracompact Hausdorff spaces are normal
statement: Every paracompact Hausdorff space is normal.
conclusion: X is normal.
typical_uses: Apply normal-space tools in paracompact Hausdorff settings.
Repair proofs that require normality of manifolds or metric-like spaces.
common_misuses: Claiming paracompact alone implies normal without separation hypotheses.
Using compact Hausdorff normality where paracompact Hausdorff is the relevant theorem.
bridge_lemmas: Locally finite refinements can separate closed sets by controlled open neighborhoods.
repair_templates: Verify Hausdorffness in addition to paracompactness before invoking normality.

name: Metric spaces are paracompact
statement: Every metric space is paracompact.
conditions: X is a metric space with its metric topology.
conclusion: Every open cover of X has a locally finite open refinement.
typical_uses: Use paracompactness in metric spaces without constructing refinements manually.
Repair arguments needing locally finite refinements in metric settings.
common_misuses: Assuming arbitrary topological spaces are paracompact.
Using metric paracompactness when the topology is not known to come from a metric.
bridge_lemmas: Metric open covers admit locally finite refinements built from distance-to-complement or well-ordered cover layers.
repair_templates: First establish metrizability or an explicit metric inducing the topology, then invoke metric paracompactness.

name: Smirnov metrization theorem
statement: A space is metrizable iff it is paracompact, Hausdorff, and locally metrizable.
conclusion: X is metrizable iff X is paracompact Hausdorff and every point has a metrizable neighborhood.
typical_uses: Prove global metrizability from local metrizability plus paracompactness.
Repair manifold metrizability arguments.
common_misuses: Assuming locally metrizable Hausdorff spaces are automatically metrizable without paracompactness.
Omitting Hausdorffness.
bridge_lemmas: Paracompactness supplies locally finite refinements that patch local metric data.
repair_templates: Add or prove paracompactness before upgrading local metrizability to metrizability.

name: Complete metric space
statement: A metric space is complete if every Cauchy sequence converges to a point of the space.
conclusion: X is complete iff every Cauchy sequence in X has a limit in X.
typical_uses: Check completeness hypotheses in Baire and compactness theorems.
Repair sequence arguments where the limit might lie in a completion rather than in the space.
common_misuses: Confusing completeness with compactness.
Letting a Cauchy sequence converge outside the space.
bridge_lemmas: Every convergent sequence is Cauchy; the converse is exactly the completeness condition.
repair_templates: Show the Cauchy sequence has a limit and verify the limit belongs to X.

name: Closed subspaces of complete metric spaces
statement: A closed subspace of a complete metric space is complete, and a complete subspace of a metric space is closed when the ambient space is metric.
conditions: A is a subspace of a metric space X.
conclusion: If X is complete and A is closed in X, then A is complete; if A is complete, then A is closed in X.
typical_uses: Prove completeness of function spaces or closed constraint sets.
Repair completeness proofs by checking closedness in a complete ambient space.
common_misuses: Assuming arbitrary subspaces of complete spaces are complete.
Claiming complete subsets are closed in non-metric settings without a metric theorem.
bridge_lemmas: A Cauchy sequence in A is Cauchy in X and converges in X; closedness forces the limit into A.
repair_templates: Add proof that the subspace is closed in the complete ambient metric space.

name: Completion of a metric space
statement: Every metric space has a completion, a complete metric space containing an isometric dense copy of the original space.
conclusion: There exists a complete metric space X_hat and an isometric embedding i:X->X_hat with dense image.
typical_uses: Repair arguments needing limits of Cauchy sequences not present in X.
Justify passing from a metric space to its completion.
common_misuses: Identifying X with its completion without noting the embedding.
Assuming completion preserves all topological or algebraic structure automatically.
bridge_lemmas: Completion can be built from equivalence classes of Cauchy sequences.
repair_templates: Embed X into its completion and then verify any extra structure or subset property separately.

name: Compact metric iff complete and totally bounded
statement: A metric space is compact iff it is complete and totally bounded.
conclusion: X is compact iff X is complete and for every epsilon>0, X is covered by finitely many epsilon-balls.
typical_uses: Prove compactness of metric spaces using finite nets and completeness.
Repair compactness proofs that show only boundedness.
common_misuses: Replacing total boundedness by ordinary boundedness in arbitrary metric spaces.
Omitting completeness.
bridge_lemmas: Total boundedness gives Cauchy subsequences; completeness gives their limits.
repair_templates: Prove finite epsilon-net coverage for every epsilon and prove Cauchy sequences converge in X.

name: Compact-open topology
statement: The compact-open topology on C(X,Y) is generated by subbasic sets of maps sending a compact subset K of X into an open subset U of Y.
conditions: X and Y are topological spaces.
conclusion: Sets S(K,U)={f in C(X,Y): f(K) subset U} form a subbasis for the compact-open topology.
typical_uses: Analyze convergence and continuity in spaces of continuous maps.
Repair function-space arguments by using compact subbasic conditions.
common_misuses: Using arbitrary subsets K instead of compact subsets.
Confusing pointwise convergence with compact-open convergence.
bridge_lemmas: Finite intersections of subbasic S(K,U) sets form basic neighborhoods.
repair_templates: Express the desired neighborhood as finitely many compact-to-open containment conditions.

name: Compact convergence
statement: For metric codomain, convergence in the compact-open topology is uniform convergence on each compact subset under standard local compactness or metric hypotheses used in the text.
conditions: f_n and f are continuous maps X->Y.
The compact-open topology is being compared with compact convergence under the hypotheses of the section.
conclusion: f_n converges to f compactly iff for every compact K subset X and epsilon>0, eventually sup_{x in K} d(f_n(x),f(x))<epsilon.
typical_uses: Repair convergence proofs in function spaces by checking uniformity on compact subsets.
Distinguish compact convergence from pointwise convergence and global uniform convergence.
common_misuses: Checking only pointwise convergence on each compact set.
Assuming compact convergence is uniform convergence on all of X when X is not compact.
bridge_lemmas: Uniform convergence on compact K controls membership in compact-open subbasic neighborhoods when the codomain is metric.
repair_templates: Fix an arbitrary compact K and prove an eventual uniform epsilon bound on K.

name: Ascoli theorem seed form
statement: For suitable compact Hausdorff or compact metric settings, an equicontinuous pointwise bounded family of functions into a metric space has compact closure in the compact-open or uniform topology as stated in the theorem version.
conditions: The domain and codomain satisfy the compactness and metric hypotheses of the Ascoli theorem version being used.
The family of functions is equicontinuous.
The family satisfies the required pointwise relative compactness or boundedness condition.
conclusion: The family has compact closure, or every sequence has a compactly convergent subsequence, according to the theorem version.
typical_uses: Repair compactness claims for families of functions.
Check missing equicontinuity or pointwise boundedness assumptions.
common_misuses: Using pointwise boundedness alone to conclude compactness.
Applying a sequential version outside metric settings.
bridge_lemmas: Equicontinuity upgrades finite control on a dense or finite net to uniform control on compact domains.
repair_templates: Add equicontinuity and pointwise compactness hypotheses before applying Ascoli.

name: Baire theorem for complete metric spaces
statement: A complete metric space is a Baire space: countable intersections of open dense sets are dense.
conditions: X is a complete metric space.
conclusion: If U_n is open dense in X for every n, then intersection_n U_n is dense in X.
typical_uses: Prove existence by showing a residual set is nonempty or dense.
Repair category arguments by adding completeness.
common_misuses: Applying Baire theorem to incomplete metric spaces without checking they are Baire.
Concluding a countable intersection of dense sets is open.
bridge_lemmas: Construct nested balls with radii tending to zero and use completeness for a limit point.
repair_templates: Verify completeness or work in a complete closed subspace before using Baire category.

name: Baire theorem for locally compact Hausdorff spaces
statement: A locally compact Hausdorff space is a Baire space.
conclusion: Every countable intersection of open dense subsets of X is dense in X.
typical_uses: Use category arguments in nonmetric locally compact spaces.
Repair proofs that invoke Baire without completeness by using local compactness.
common_misuses: Omitting Hausdorffness or local compactness.
Concluding that arbitrary intersections of dense open sets are dense.
bridge_lemmas: Local compactness supplies nested open sets with compact closures.
repair_templates: Check local compact Hausdorff hypotheses, then apply the Baire-space conclusion.

name: Nowhere dense and first category
statement: A set is nowhere dense if the interior of its closure is empty; a set is of first category if it is a countable union of nowhere dense sets.
conditions: A is a subset of a topological space X.
conclusion: A is nowhere dense iff int(cl(A)) is empty; A is first category iff A is a countable union of nowhere dense subsets.
typical_uses: Translate Baire category arguments into dense open complements.
Repair proofs that confuse dense complement with nowhere dense.
common_misuses: Assuming every set with empty interior is nowhere dense.
Using uncountable unions in the definition of first category.
bridge_lemmas: A is nowhere dense iff X\cl(A) is open dense.
repair_templates: Prove empty interior of the closure, not just empty interior of the set.

name: Homotopy of maps
statement: Two maps f,g:X->Y are homotopic if there is a continuous map H:X x I->Y with H(x,0)=f(x) and H(x,1)=g(x).
conditions: H:X x I->Y is continuous with the stated endpoint values.
conclusion: f is homotopic to g.
typical_uses: Show maps induce the same algebraic invariant under homotopy.
Repair homotopy claims by checking continuity on the product.
common_misuses: Specifying pointwise paths H(x,t) without proving H is jointly continuous.
Changing endpoints or basepoints when a relative homotopy is needed.
bridge_lemmas: The product topology on X x I is used for continuity of H.
repair_templates: Define H on all of X x I and verify endpoint equations and continuity.

name: Path homotopy relative endpoints
statement: Two paths from x0 to x1 are path homotopic if a homotopy between them keeps both endpoints fixed for all time.
conditions: f,g:I->X are paths with f(0)=g(0)=x0 and f(1)=g(1)=x1.
conclusion: f and g are path homotopic relative endpoints.
typical_uses: Form well-defined products in the fundamental group.
Repair homotopies of loops that move the basepoint.
common_misuses: Using ordinary homotopy of paths while endpoints move.
Forgetting endpoint conditions when multiplying path classes.
bridge_lemmas: Path homotopy relative endpoints is an equivalence relation.
repair_templates: Modify or replace the homotopy so endpoints stay fixed throughout.

name: Path product laws up to homotopy
statement: Concatenation of paths is well-defined on path-homotopy classes and is associative up to path homotopy; constant paths act as identities and reversed paths as inverses.
conditions: Paths have matching endpoints for concatenation.
conclusion: Path-homotopy classes of loops at a basepoint form a group under concatenation.
typical_uses: Justify algebraic manipulation in fundamental groups.
Repair path concatenation proofs by checking endpoint matching.
common_misuses: Concatenating paths whose endpoint and startpoint do not match.
Treating concatenation as strictly associative as parametrized paths rather than associative up to homotopy.
bridge_lemmas: Reparametrization of a path is path homotopic to the original path when endpoints are fixed.
repair_templates: Pass to path-homotopy classes before applying group laws.

name: Fundamental group
statement: The fundamental group pi_1(X,x0) is the group of path-homotopy classes of loops in X based at x0 under concatenation.
conditions: x0 is a point of X.
Loops are paths f:I->X with f(0)=f(1)=x0.
conclusion: The set of path-homotopy classes of based loops is a group pi_1(X,x0).
typical_uses: Translate loop homotopy information into group calculations.
Repair proofs by tracking basepoints and loop classes.
common_misuses: Ignoring the basepoint in spaces that are not path connected.
Using free homotopy of loops instead of based path homotopy.
bridge_lemmas: The constant loop is the identity and the reversed loop gives inverses.
repair_templates: Specify the basepoint and use endpoint-fixed homotopies for loop classes.

name: Basepoint change isomorphism
statement: A path from x0 to x1 induces an isomorphism between pi_1(X,x0) and pi_1(X,x1) by conjugating loops along that path.
